title: "Non-warrantable": the word that can stall a Florida condo sale, and what it really means
description: What makes a Florida condo building non-warrantable under Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac rules, how it affects a sale or refinance, and what to ask.
dek: Your unit can be in perfect shape and still fail a lender's check, because the lender is judging the whole building. Here is what "non-warrantable" means, the most common reasons a building lands there, and what changes it.

body.text: A buyer loves your condo. The inspection is clean. Then the lender calls and says the building is "non-warrantable," and the deal slows down or falls apart. Many Florida owners hear that word for the first time at exactly this moment.

This is a plain-words guide to what the word means and which rules sit behind it. It is not legal or lending advice. For your own unit, talk with a mortgage lender, your manager or board, and if needed your association attorney.

body.title: Terms to know
body.text: Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac: two companies that buy most ordinary home loans from lenders. Conventional loan: a regular mortgage that meets their rules. Warrantable: lender shorthand for a condo building that meets Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac building rules, so a conventional loan can be sold to them. Non-warrantable: a building that does not meet those rules. It is an industry word, not a legal label from the state.
Why the lender looks at the whole building

When you buy a house, the lender mostly cares about that house. With a condo, every owner shares the roof, the structure, the budget and the insurance. If the building has trouble, every unit feels it. So before a lender can sell a condo loan to Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac, it checks the project as a whole.

If the building fails that check, the loan cannot go to Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac. The buyer may still be able to borrow, but usually from a lender that keeps the loan itself, often on different terms. Some buyers will need to pay cash. Fewer possible buyers can mean a longer sale. The same check applies when an owner wants to refinance.
The most common reasons a building is non-warrantable
Fannie Mae lists "ineligible project" traits in its Selling Guide, section B4-2.1-03. The version posted November 4, 2026 includes these, among others:

items: Critical repairs that are not done (more on this below).
An evacuation order, until the unsafe condition is fixed and the building is deemed safe to live in.

Pending lawsuits against the association over safety, structural soundness, habitability or use. Some minor cases can still qualify, for example when expected damages and legal costs are not expected to top 10% of the project's funded reserves.
One person or company owning too many units. For a building of 21 or more units, the limit is 20% of the units.
Commercial or mixed-use space above 35% of the project or building.
Running like a hotel: rental pooling, hotel-type services, documents that limit owner occupancy, or marketing as a hotel or investment.
A building that is terminating (being dissolved as a condo) or in insolvency proceedings.
A status of "Unavailable" in Fannie Mae's Condo Project Manager system, which lenders check.

body.text: The critical repair rule, in plain words

For many Florida buildings working through milestone inspections and structural integrity reserve studies (SIRS), this is the rule that matters most. A milestone inspection is the state-required structural check of older condo buildings three stories or taller. A SIRS is the study that sets how much the association must save for the building's major parts.

Fannie Mae defines critical repairs as repairs or replacements that significantly affect the safety, soundness, structural integrity or habitability of the building, or its financial health or marketability. Its examples include:

items: Defects that could cause a key building system to fail within one year if not fixed.
Mold, water intrusion or damaging leaks.
Advanced physical deterioration.
Failing a state, county or local mandatory inspection about structural safety, soundness or habitability.

Unfunded repairs costing more than $10,000 per unit that should be done within the next 12 months. Fannie Mae says this does not include repairs owners make themselves or repairs paid for by a special assessment.

body.text: Fannie Mae names items to look at, such as sea walls, elevators, waterproofing, stairwells, balconies, foundations, electrical systems and parking garages.

Two more points trip up many owners. First, if a structural or mechanical inspection from the last three years shows critical repairs that have not been addressed, Fannie Mae says the building stays ineligible until the repairs are completed and documented. The lender then reviews an engineer's report or similar document showing the problem is resolved. Second, if a special assessment is for a critical repair and the repair is not done yet, the building is ineligible.

Freddie Mac's condo FAQ says much the same: an association loan or a special assessment is an acceptable way to pay, but "regardless of the means of funding," loans in projects needing critical repairs stay ineligible until the repairs are completed. Freddie Mac also says a building that failed a local inspection stays ineligible until the required repairs or inspection report are completed and documented.

body.title: The short version
body.text: Raising the money is not enough. For Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac, the building usually becomes eligible again when the critical work is finished and documented.

items: Planning to sell or refinance? Call a lender before you list or apply, and ask whether your building is currently eligible for conventional loans.
Ask your manager in writing whether any milestone inspection or other structural report lists repairs that are not finished, and when the work is expected to be done.
Ask whether a special assessment now being collected is for safety or structural work. If so, a buyer's lender may treat the building as ineligible until the work is complete.
If you are told the building is ineligible, ask the lender which rule it failed. The fix depends on the reason.

body.text: If you are a board member:

items: Ask your manager how the association answers lender questionnaires, and who checks those answers. Buyers' lenders rely on them.
Keep an engineer's letter or report on file when critical repairs are finished. Fannie Mae says lenders review that kind of document.
Share the repair schedule with owners. Many sales hinge on when work will be complete.
Questions about lawsuits, documents or termination belong with your association attorney.

body.text: Not every non-warrantable building has a problem. A building can be non-warrantable because it has a lot of commercial space or because one investor owns many units. The label describes lending rules, not whether the building is safe.

faq.q: What does non-warrantable condo mean in Florida?
faq.a: It is lender shorthand for a condo building that does not meet Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac project rules, so a conventional loan in that building cannot be sold to them. Buyers may still borrow from lenders that keep their own loans, or pay cash.

faq.q: Can I refinance my condo if the building is non-warrantable?
faq.a: Not with a loan sold to Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac, because the same building review applies to refinances. Some lenders offer loans they keep themselves. Ask a lender which options fit your building.

faq.q: Does a special assessment make a condo non-warrantable?
faq.a: Not by itself. Under Fannie Mae's rules, a building is ineligible if a special assessment is for a critical repair that has not been fixed yet. Freddie Mac says safety-related repairs must be fully completed.

faq.q: How does a Florida condo become warrantable again after repairs?
faq.a: For critical repairs, both Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac look for the repairs to be completed and documented, such as with an engineer's report. Other reasons, like too much commercial space, need a different fix. Ask the lender which rule the building failed.

faq.q: What is the $10,000 per unit rule for condo repairs?
faq.a: Fannie Mae counts unfunded repairs costing more than $10,000 per unit that should be done within 12 months as a critical repair. Repairs paid for by a special assessment or done by unit owners are not counted under that item.
